Ruby
ROO-bee
noun
Hebrew peninim (H6443) — traditionally translated "rubies" in older English versions, though the Hebrew likely refers to coral, pearls, or red corals rather than the corundum-gem ruby of modern jewelry. Used in Scripture as the benchmark of human-valuable preciousness against which wisdom, the virtuous woman, and the price of a soul are measured (and exceeded).

📖 Biblical Definition

Ruby (Hebrew peninim) appears in Scripture as the BENCHMARK of preciousness against which higher things are measured — and always EXCEEDED. "The price of wisdom is above rubies" (Job 28:18). "She [wisdom] is more precious than rubies" (Prov 3:15). "For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it" (Prov 8:11). "My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver" (Prov 8:19). "For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold" (Prov 3:14). And in Proverbs 31, the climactic biblical portrait of feminine virtue: "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies" (Prov 31:10). The Hebrew peninim may not refer to corundum-ruby specifically — many scholars hold it means red coral, or pearls, or the deep-red stones available in the ancient Near East. But the canonical function is consistent: peninim is what people PAY MOST for, and Scripture uses it always to introduce something WORTH MORE — wisdom, the godly wife, the price of a soul. The economic theology is clear: the world esteems certain things as supremely precious; God then names a category of greater preciousness BEYOND what the world prizes. To know wisdom is to recognize what is truly above rubies; to find a virtuous wife is to receive what cannot be bought even with the world's most precious commodity. Christ Himself is the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:30) — the unpurchasable above-rubies treasure that God gives freely to those who ask in faith.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A precious red stone (Hebrew probably coral, pearls, or red corals rather than corundum ruby); the biblical benchmark of preciousness against which wisdom, virtue, and the soul are weighed and exceeded.

RUBY, noun. A precious red stone, in modern jewelry the red variety of corundum. The Hebrew peninim, traditionally translated rubies in older English versions, may refer to red coral, pearls, or other deep-red precious materials of the ancient Near East.

In Scripture, used always as the benchmark of preciousness against which higher things (wisdom, the virtuous woman, the soul) are measured and exceeded: Job 28:18; Prov 3:15; 8:11; 20:15; 31:10.

📖 Key Scripture

Proverbs 31:10 — "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies."

Proverbs 8:11 — "For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it."

Job 28:18 — "No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies."

Proverbs 3:15 — "She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Ruby is corrupted when modern translations remove the consistent "above rubies" rhetoric (replacing rubies with pearls or coral in ways that lose the canonical chorus), or when the Proverbs 31 "price above rubies" is sentimentalized as flattery rather than as serious economic theology about the actual worth of a godly wife.

expand to see more

Translation-chorus loss. The Hebrew peninim ALWAYS introduces a comparison: this thing is ABOVE the highest-priced commodity. When modern translations swap "rubies" for "pearls" or "coral" or "jewels" in different passages, the reader misses that ONE consistent word is being used as the benchmark across Job, Proverbs, and other wisdom texts. Whether or not modern crystallography matches peninim to ruby specifically, the canonical pattern of consistent comparison is what matters.

Sentimental Proverbs 31. "Her price is far above rubies" is sometimes Mother's Day-flattened into mere romantic flattery for wives. But the text is serious economic theology: a godly wife is OBJECTIVELY MORE VALUABLE than the world's most precious commodity. The Hebrew peninim in Job 28 stood as the highest-priced thing humans could buy; Proverbs 31 says a virtuous woman exceeds even that. This is not a poetic compliment; it is a price valuation. Husbands who treat their wives as accessories or burdens have failed to count what they actually possess. Daughters considering future husbands have a metric: am I being sought as a far-above-rubies treasure or as a possession to be priced down?

Hebrew peninim (H6443) — traditionally rubies; likely red coral, pearls, or red stones; the biblical benchmark of preciousness.

Hebrew peninim (H6443) — rubies; traditionally rendered "rubies" in older English (KJV), though Hebrew may mean red coral, pearls, or red stones

Used in Scripture always as the benchmark of preciousness against which higher things are measured and EXCEEDED

Canonical chorus: wisdom > rubies (Job 28:18; Prov 3:15; 8:11); virtuous wife > rubies (Prov 31:10)

The world's most-priced commodity is the floor, not the ceiling, of God's economy of preciousness

Usage

"Her price is far above rubies — the virtuous wife is the canonical above-the-benchmark treasure."

"Wisdom is more precious than rubies — the Bible names what the world prizes most, only to point past it to what God prizes more."

"If you have a godly wife, you possess what cannot be priced; if you have wisdom, you possess what cannot be bought."
